title: Grace and merit (CCC 2006–2011)
hookLine: even our merits are God's gifts

lines: A MUG FROM THE DOLLAR STORE.
cards: A seven-year-old comes home from the dollar store with a birthday present for her father: a mug that says world's okayest dad, wrapped in the comics page with far too much tape. He opens it and acts as if it's gold.

Nobody mentions that the money for the mug came from him, and so did the ride to the store. In a sense, he paid for his own present. And still, the gift is completely hers, and he's completely delighted.

teach.b: Back in year one you met grace itself. Today, what grace does with our work. Merit, the Catechism says, is the reward a community owes someone for what they've done: fair pay for fair work.
Then it turns the word around. Before God, nobody has a strict right to merit anything. The gap between Creator and creature is too wide; everything we have, we first received.
So where does merit come from? From God's free plan to bring people into the work of his grace.
Grace goes first: the free gift that makes a good act possible. Then the person freely says yes and acts, and God, who gave the strength, rewards the act.
The order matters: the merit of good works belongs first to God's grace, and then to the person who acted. The Catechism quotes Augustine, paraphrased: our merits are God's gifts.
And a prayer of the Mass: in crowning the merits of his saints, God crowns his own gifts. Paul says it in the Douay-Rheims: "By the grace of God, I am what I am."
He worked harder than the others, he adds, yet not he, but God's grace with him. The Catechism calls the charity of Christ the source in us of all our merits.

And it gives the last word to Thérèse of Lisieux, who wrote that at the evening of her life she would come before God with empty hands, not asking him to count her works, and wanting to be clothed in his own justice.
Merit isn't a ledger. It's a gift that becomes ours, and then goes home.

how: Catholics are taught that every good work begins with God's grace; some end the day with an examen, thanking God for the good done and asking pardon for the rest.

o: a reward God owes anyone who works hard enough
points earned with God by piling up good deeds
God's gift goes first; the good we do with it is rewarded

p: what a community owes for what you did
the free gift that goes first

s: Catholic teaching says we can earn heaven by piling up good works
the Catechism says nobody has a strict right to merit before God; merit comes from his free plan and his grace.
the Catechism says our merits are themselves God's gifts
it quotes Augustine: our merits are God's gifts.
in Catholic teaching, a good act done with grace is still partly ours

games.q: you're Paul, writing to the Corinthians. you've worked harder than the others. how do you describe it?
o: I did it on my own strength.
by the grace of God I am what I am: I worked, yet God's grace with me.
I did nothing; it was all God and none of me.
games.why: Paul holds both: he labored, and it was God's grace with him. that both-at-once is the heart of Catholic teaching on merit.

practice: Think back over the last few days to one good thing you actually did, maybe small, a call returned, a hard truth said kindly.
See it plainly, without shrinking or polishing it, and ask where it came from: the strength, the moment, the person who taught you how.
If you pray, thank God for it as his gift working in you; if not, simply hold it with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Grace and merit. Grace goes first, a free gift; merit is the good we freely do with it, counted first to his grace and then to us. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: favor, a free gift; the Church's word for grace.

carryVoice: Your line: his gift in us. Thanks can be yours and his at once. Until tomorrow.
